newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: "Old" Zaire delegation seats in UN are as before.
newsitem.headline: "Old" Zaire delegation seats in UN are as before.

text.p: The Zairean delegation chosen by the government of ousted President Mobutu Sese Seko took its old seats on Tuesday in the General Assembly without challenge, assembly officials said.
The meeting to elect judges to the Yugoslav war crimes tribunal was the first assembly session since forces of Laurent Kabila captured Kinshasa over the weekend.

The delegation, some of whose envoys said they have not received salaries in five years, will remain as representatives of Zaire until a government formed by victorious Laurent Kabila hands in its credentials or other U.N. members dispute its right to be there.

Spokesman Fred Eckhard said the United Nations would not be in a posiion to change the name of Zaire in the world body until it received notification "from the recognised authorities in that country."
Kabila, rejecting the name chosen by Mobutu, renamed the country the Democratic Republic of Congo -- its name between 1964 and 1971.

De facto U.N. recognition means presenting credentials of a new chief delegate as well as a name change. Unless challenged, approval is nearly certain in the assembly's credential's committee -- after what Eckhard calls a "critical mass" of states have recognised the Kabila government.
He said this usually meant that enough governments had accepted the new Kinshasa authorities so that the General Assembly or any of its committees do not have to make a decision.
"Governments recognise other governments," Eckhard said. "This is not a matter for the United Nations to decide."

Seating in the assembly is according to the English alphabet. The new government could decide to sit under "D' for "democratic" or under "C" for Congo, next to its smaller neighbour, the Republic of the Congo.
That country, whose capital is Brazzaville, has yet to make an official response to the sudden reappearance of a country with the same name next door.
